description: A large evergreen to semi-deciduous tree up to 25-30 m with a buttressed trunk, smooth grey-white bark that peels in flakes, oblong leaves, spikes of small cream flowers and distinctive fruits with five longitudinal wings.
cultural_significance: The tree takes its name from the epic hero Arjuna in popular tradition, and the bark is the best-known Ayurvedic heart tonic. Often seen beside rivers and streams in India.
habitat: Riverbanks, streams and moist deciduous forests of the Indian subcontinent; often planted along water channels and roadsides.

uses.title: Hridaya (heart) tonic
uses.detail: Stem bark is described as Hridya, traditionally taken as a decoction in milk to support the heart and circulation.

uses.title: Bone and wound healing
uses.detail: Bark powder is traditionally used internally and as a paste for fractures (Bhagna sandhanakara) and wounds.

uses.title: Diarrhoea and dysentery
uses.detail: Its astringent bark is traditionally used in loose motions and bleeding conditions.

uses.title: Cardiovascular research
uses.detail: Studies on bark extract report effects on cholesterol and heart function; evidence is promising but not conclusive.

preparations.name: Arjuna ksheerapaka
preparations.method: Simmer bark powder in milk and water until the water evaporates; strain and take warm.
preparations.note: A classical heart-supporting preparation; use under practitioner guidance.

preparations.name: Bark churna (powder)
preparations.method: Dried bark ground to fine powder and taken with water or honey.
preparations.note: Traditional dosing is set by a practitioner.

preparations.name: Arjunarishta
preparations.method: A fermented herbal tonic prepared from bark, raisins and mahua flowers.

preparations.name: Bark paste
preparations.method: Bark paste with water or honey applied to wounds or fractures as a poultice.

precautions: May affect blood pressure, heart rate and blood clotting, so people with heart disease or on cardiac, blood-pressure, anticoagulant or diabetes medicines must consult a doctor before use and must not replace prescribed treatment. Avoid during pregnancy and lactation unless advised. High-tannin bark may cause constipation or stomach upset.

cultivation.soil: Moist alluvial or loamy soil near water
cultivation.water: High; thrives near streams and with regular watering
cultivation.harvest: Bark is traditionally harvested from mature trees; sustainable stripping is important

conservation_status: Not globally threatened; bark over-harvesting has caused local decline.
fun_fact: The tree's smooth, pale bark peels naturally in thin sheets, which is one way to recognise it along riverbanks.
